scenes.tts: Every action potential lets potassium out of the neuron. When a small patch of brain fires hard, a lot of potassium leaks out. The space between brain cells is narrow. So the potassium can build up there. A neuron's resting voltage depends largely on potassium. Something has to put it back.
scenes.visual: Two large neurons with a narrow gap; they flash and blue potassium dots collect in the gap; a question mark ends the scene.
scenes.narration: Every action potential lets potassium out of the neuron. When a small patch of brain fires hard, a lot of potassium leaks out. The space between brain cells is narrow. scenes.tts: Take an illustrative neuron with one hundred forty millimolar potassium inside. At rest, three millimolar potassium sits outside. E K is then minus one hundred two point six millivolts. After intense firing, suppose a small space reaches twelve millimolar. E K becomes minus sixty five point six millivolts. That is thirty seven millivolts more positive. A real neuron's resting voltage moves less, but in the same direction, toward threshold.
scenes.caption: Take an illustrative neuron with 140 mM potassium inside. At rest, 3 mM potassium sits outside. EK is then −102.6 mV. After intense firing, suppose a small space reaches 12 mM. EK becomes −65.6 mV. That is 37.0 mV more positive. A real neuron's resting voltage moves less, but in the same direction, toward threshold.
scenes.visual: A cell with outside potassium 3 then 12 mM; a voltage axis with the EK marker jumping from minus 102.6 to minus 65.6 and a 37.0 mV arrow.

scenes.tts: Astrocytes, a kind of glial cell, do a large share of that work. They use spatial buffering. Potassium enters an astrocyte where the outside concentration is high. It travels through that astrocyte, and through the network of astrocytes joined to it by gap junctions. It leaves where the concentration is low. Think of a sponge that soaks up a spill at one end and wrings out at the other.
scenes.visual: Two astrocytes joined by gap junctions; a blue potassium dot enters on the high side, crosses both cells, and leaves on the low side.

scenes.tts: The entry channel is largely K I R four point one, an inwardly rectifying potassium channel. Separately, the sodium potassium ATPase brings potassium into glia for net uptake. Redistribution and net uptake are distinct mechanisms.
scenes.caption: The entry channel is largely Kir4.1, an inwardly rectifying potassium channel. Separately, the sodium-potassium ATPase brings potassium into glia for net uptake. Redistribution and net uptake are distinct mechanisms.
scenes.visual: Two membrane panels: a Kir4.1 chip passing potassium in for redistribution, and an ATPase chip bringing potassium in for net uptake.
scenes.narration: The entry channel is largely Kir4.1, an inwardly rectifying potassium channel. Separately, the sodium-potassium ATPase brings potassium into glia for net uptake. Redistribution and net uptake are distinct mechanisms.

scenes.tts: Ken McCarthy's laboratory tested the channel with genetics. They used a conditional knockout driven by a glial promoter. Djukic and colleagues deleted K I R four point one from glia. In hippocampal slices from mice fifteen to twenty days old, C A one astrocytes took up potassium poorly. The deletion began in development, and it also reached oligodendrocytes. So the result cannot be pinned on mature astrocytes alone.
scenes.caption: Ken McCarthy's laboratory tested the channel with genetics. They used a conditional knockout driven by a glial promoter. Djukic and colleagues deleted Kir4.1 from glia. In hippocampal slices from mice 15 to 20 days old, CA1 astrocytes took up potassium poorly. The deletion began in development, and it also reached oligodendrocytes. So the result cannot be pinned on mature astrocytes alone.
scenes.visual: An astrocyte with Kir4.1 takes up potassium well; the channel is deleted and uptake falls; an oligodendrocyte is also marked as hit.

scenes.tts: Keep this rule. When neurons fire hard, potassium can build up outside them, and E K becomes more positive. The real resting voltage moves the same way, toward threshold, but less. Astrocytes pass that potassium through their network, from where it is high to where it is low. That is redistribution. Net uptake by the sodium potassium ATPase is a separate mechanism.
